lesson.title: Split Horizon: Do Not Tell a Neighbor What You Learned From Them
lesson.summary: Split horizon is a distance vector fix that stops a router from advertising a route back to the very neighbor it learned that route from, removing one of the simplest ways stale information can loop.
lesson.body:
Look again at the count to infinity example and notice something a little absurd: C told B that it could reach A at cost 2, using a route that went through B in the first place. B then, in effect, believed a rumor that traced straight back to itself. Split horizon is a simple rule aimed directly at that absurdity: a router should never advertise a route back to the neighbor from which it learned that route. If C's only path to A runs through B, then telling B about that path is worse than useless, since B already knows everything C knows about it, and possibly more.

Applying split horizon to the earlier scenario changes the outcome. C's route to A was learned from B, so with split horizon in place, C simply never advertises a route to A when sending updates to B, whether or not the A to B link has failed. When the link does fail, B loses its direct route and has no stale claim from C to mistakenly adopt, because C was never advertising A back to B in the first place. B correctly and immediately concludes it has no route to A, rather than looping through a slowly climbing hop count.

Split horizon is inexpensive, requires no new message types, and eliminates every two router routing loop, exactly the pattern in the A, B, C example. It does not, however, eliminate every count to infinity scenario. Picture a slightly bigger topology: routers B, C, and D, all with routes to A that ultimately depend on each other in a longer chain or a small loop running through more than two routers. Stale information can travel from B to C to D and back to B without ever violating the split horizon rule at any single hop, since split horizon only blocks a route from bouncing directly back to the one neighbor it came from, not from circulating through a longer path. Split horizon meaningfully reduces how often count to infinity occurs, and it is standard practice in distance vector protocols like RIP, but it is a mitigation, not a complete guarantee against routing loops.
